answers.text: For example, when a supplier confirms a delivery, I would just tell the assistant: always answer in three lines, in the same order every time — date, what was delivered, and if anything changed from the order. That way it always looks the same.
In my work I do something similar with claims. I would say: list every claim on its own line, with date, amount, category and who submitted it, always in that order, and put the total at the bottom.

Reading this again, the price side looks fine to me — 100 times 48.50 makes 4,850, so that is correct. But something about the dates feels off — the call was on the 14th and then it talks about three days from today for the 19th, and that does not quite fit. I would want to look at it again before sending.
62 up from 54, I make that about 15%, so that number is fine. The rest of it — the on-time rate and the stock split — reads okay to me at a glance.

I would sign off on the second one, because it shows the numbers behind it — 612,000 in sales and 25,100 in returns — not just the 4.1%. The first one just gives the percentage with nothing behind it, so there is no way to see where it comes from.
I would send the second reply, since it has the order number and the credit reference in it, not just a general sorry. The first one sounds nice but there is nothing in it you could actually look up.
1. No. 2. Yes. 3. No. 4. No, better not risk it. 5. No.
I would leave out the pricing and discount numbers, and be careful with the part naming both companies in the confidentiality clause — that feels like something that should stay internal.
Before it goes out, I would check the totals against warehouse numbers myself, every week, before it goes to the manager.
Step one is where I would be careful, because if the assistant reads the order wrong at the start, everything after that follows the mistake.
